title: Bowling Alone
text:
In 1995 the political scientist Robert Putnam of Harvard published an essay with a striking image: more Americans were bowling than ever, but fewer were bowling in leagues. In 2000 he expanded it into the book Bowling Alone, drawing on surveys, membership records and other data covering several decades of American life.

Putnam documented a broad decline, starting around the 1960s and 1970s, in what he called social capital: the networks of relationships, trust and shared norms that let people cooperate. Membership in groups like parent-teacher associations, labor unions, fraternal clubs and civic organizations had fallen. People attended fewer public meetings, entertained friends at home less often, joined fewer picnics and card games, and reported trusting others less. Some forms of participation had grown, such as mailing-list organizations and self-help groups, but these often asked little more than writing a check.

He looked at several possible causes, including busier work lives, suburban sprawl and long commutes, and especially television, which kept people at home in the evening. The largest factor, he argued, was generational: the civic-minded generation that came of age around the Second World War was being replaced by generations that joined less. Putnam linked high social capital to better schools, safer neighborhoods, better health and more responsive government.
lesson: Community is built by showing up: joining, attending, hosting. Belonging to something beyond your home and work benefits you and everyone around you.
source: Putnam, R. D. (2000). Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community. Simon and Schuster.
caveat: Critics have disputed how steep the decline was and argued that new forms of association, including online ones, replaced some of what was lost.
